items.prompt: A team says 'we changed the database schema but didn't touch the API contract.' What does that most likely mean?
choices: They restructured the internal database, but the request/response shape clients see is unchanged
They forgot to update their documentation
The API is now faster
Clients will need to update their code
items.explanation: The API contract is about what a client can observe and depend on — field names, types, required/optional, endpoint shape. Internal implementation, including the database schema, is free to change as long as the observable contract stays the same.
items.reference:
In the contract

Field names, types, required/optional, endpoint/operation shape

Not in the contract

Internal implementation, DB schema, code structure

Why: a client can only depend on what the request/response shape promises — internals are free to change as long as that shape holds.

items.prompt: Where does an API's contract actually 'live,' in the sense that matters for deciding whether a change is safe?
choices: In the currently-deployed clients' assumptions about the response shape, not just in a design doc
Only in the OpenAPI/GraphQL schema file in the repo
In the server's internal code comments
It doesn't live anywhere until a client complains
items.explanation: A design doc or schema file describes the contract, but what actually determines whether a change is safe is what deployed clients rely on right now — a doc can be technically accurate and a change can still break real traffic if clients depend on something the doc never mentioned.
items.reference:
In the contract

Field names, types, required/optional, endpoint/operation shape

Not in the contract

Internal implementation, DB schema, code structure

Why: a client can only depend on what the request/response shape promises — internals are free to change as long as that shape holds.

items.prompt: Which of these counts as part of an API's contract with its clients?
choices: Field names, their types, and whether each is required or optional
Which programming language the server is written in
How the server's code is organized into files
The name of the internal function that handles the request
items.explanation: The contract is exactly the observable request/response shape — field names, types, required/optional status, status codes, endpoint/operation existence. Everything about how the server is implemented internally is invisible to clients and free to change.
items.reference:
In the contract

Field names, types, required/optional, endpoint/operation shape

Not in the contract

Internal implementation, DB schema, code structure

Why: a client can only depend on what the request/response shape promises — internals are free to change as long as that shape holds.

items.prompt: A server renames a response field from userName to username (lowercase n). Is this breaking?
choices: Yes — any client reading userName now gets undefined
No — it's just a casing fix
Only if the client uses TypeScript
Only if the field was required
items.explanation: A rename is functionally identical to removing the old field and adding a new one — from an existing client's point of view, the field it reads is simply gone. Looking like a small cosmetic change doesn't change that.
items.reference:
ChangeBreaking?
Add optional fieldNo
Remove/rename a field a client readsYes
Change a field's typeYes
Make an optional field requiredYes

Why: the test is always whether an existing, unmodified client keeps working after the change.

items.prompt: A server adds a new optional discountPercent field to an existing order response, alongside all the fields already there. Is this breaking?
choices: No — old clients that don't read the new field are unaffected
Yes — any new field changes the response
Only if discountPercent is a number
Yes — because the response got larger
items.explanation: Old clients only read the fields they know about; a field they never look for being present alongside the ones they do read has no effect on them. This is the additive, non-breaking half of API evolution.
items.reference:
ChangeBreaking?
Add optional fieldNo
Remove/rename a field a client readsYes
Change a field's typeYes
Make an optional field requiredYes

Why: the test is always whether an existing, unmodified client keeps working after the change.

items.prompt: A server changes a previously-optional shippingAddress field to be required on every order-creation request. Is this breaking?
choices: Yes — old clients that omit it will now get requests rejected
No — most orders include it anyway
Only if shippingAddress was a string before
No — required fields are safer
items.explanation: Tightening a constraint (optional to required) rejects requests that used to succeed. Any old client that legitimately omitted the field — even rarely — starts failing the moment this ships.
items.reference:
ChangeBreaking?
Add optional fieldNo
Remove/rename a field a client readsYes
Change a field's typeYes
Make an optional field requiredYes

Why: the test is always whether an existing, unmodified client keeps working after the change.

items.prompt: Why is adding a brand-new endpoint, like GET /users/:id/badges, considered safe with zero coordination?
choices: No existing client was calling it before, so nothing can depend on its absence
New endpoints are always faster than old ones
It doesn't require a database change
Clients automatically discover new endpoints
items.explanation: A client can only be broken by a change to something it actually depends on. Since nothing existed at that URL before, no client could have built a dependency on it — there's nothing to break.
items.reference:
✅ New optional field — old clients ignore it
✅ New endpoint/query — nothing depended on it yet

Why: a client can only break on something it actually reads or requires — unread additions are invisible to it.

items.prompt: A new, optional query parameter ?includeArchived=true is added to an existing search endpoint, defaulting to the old behavior when omitted. Why is this safe?
choices: Existing clients that never send the parameter keep getting exactly the old behavior
Query parameters can't affect responses
It only affects archived data, which nobody uses
GET requests can't be breaking by definition
items.explanation: The key phrase is 'defaulting to the old behavior' — an old client that doesn't know the parameter exists never sends it, so it silently gets the same behavior it always got. The moment a default changes existing behavior instead of preserving it, this stops being safe.
items.reference:
✅ New optional field — old clients ignore it
✅ New endpoint/query — nothing depended on it yet

Why: a client can only break on something it actually reads or requires — unread additions are invisible to it.

items.prompt: In REST, what typically identifies a resource and how you can act on it?
choices: A URL (the noun) combined with an HTTP verb (the action)
A single query string naming the fields wanted
A GraphQL type definition
The response's Content-Type header alone
items.explanation: REST's core idea is resources as nouns (URLs like /users/42) manipulated through a small, fixed set of verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) — the URL + verb pair is what identifies the operation.
items.reference:
REST

Resources (URLs) + verbs, fixed response shape per endpoint

GraphQL

One typed schema, client selects exact fields per query

Why: same underlying goal — describe what a client can depend on — expressed two different ways.

items.prompt: In GraphQL, what determines the shape of a response?
choices: Whatever fields the client's query explicitly selects
A fixed shape defined per endpoint
The HTTP verb used
The order fields were added to the schema
items.explanation: GraphQL inverts REST's fixed-shape-per-endpoint model — the schema defines everything that's queryable, but the actual response shape on any given call is determined by which fields that specific query selected.
items.reference:
REST

Resources (URLs) + verbs, fixed response shape per endpoint

GraphQL

One typed schema, client selects exact fields per query

Why: same underlying goal — describe what a client can depend on — expressed two different ways.

items.prompt: A REST endpoint GET /users/42 always returns the full user object, even if a screen only needs the user's name. What is this an example of?
choices: Over-fetching — the response includes more than the client needs
Under-fetching — the response is missing data
A breaking change
A required-field violation
items.explanation: Over-fetching is receiving more data than needed because the endpoint's shape is fixed rather than selectable — the opposite problem, under-fetching, is needing multiple requests because a fixed shape doesn't include enough nested data in one call.
items.reference:
REST

Resources (URLs) + verbs, fixed response shape per endpoint

GraphQL

One typed schema, client selects exact fields per query

Why: same underlying goal — describe what a client can depend on — expressed two different ways.

items.prompt: What does API versioning fundamentally let a team do that they couldn't do otherwise?
choices: Run an old and a new contract at the same time, so existing clients keep working during a transition
Avoid ever making a breaking change
Skip writing tests for new features
Automatically update every client's code
items.explanation: Versioning doesn't prevent breaking changes — it lets two contracts coexist so clients on the old one keep working while new clients (or an eventual forced migration) move to the new one. It's a transition mechanism, not a way to avoid change.
items.reference:
⏳ Versioning runs an old and new contract at the same time — it buys existing clients time, it doesn't avoid the change.

Why: without it, a breaking change would force every client to upgrade instantly, which isn't realistic for mobile apps, integrations, or third parties.

items.prompt: Why not just ship a breaking change directly, without any version, and let clients update whenever they notice?
choices: Some clients (old app installs, unattended integrations) can't update on the server's schedule, so they'd simply break
HTTP doesn't allow breaking changes
Breaking changes are always illegal in production APIs
Clients automatically retry until they get the new shape
items.explanation: Not every client can upgrade the moment the server changes — a mobile app install can't force-update overnight, and an unattended integration might not notice a change for months. Versioning exists precisely because 'just tell clients to update' isn't realistic on the server's timeline.
items.reference:
⏳ Versioning runs an old and new contract at the same time — it buys existing clients time, it doesn't avoid the change.

Why: without it, a breaking change would force every client to upgrade instantly, which isn't realistic for mobile apps, integrations, or third parties.

items.prompt: In the shared-core-plus-adapters pattern, why do /v1 and /v2 both call the same underlying function instead of having separate implementations?
choices: So a bug fix or business-logic change only needs to be made in one place
Because REST requires it
To make the API slower on purpose
Because GraphQL doesn't support this pattern
items.explanation: Forking implementation per version means every future fix or business-rule change has to be applied, tested, and deployed separately for each supported version — and versions can silently drift apart from each other. Routing through one shared core avoids both problems.
items.reference:
🧩 /v1 and /v2 adapters both call the SAME shared core logic
🛠️ A bug fix in core applies to both versions at once

Why: forking the codebase per version means every future fix has to be applied N times, and versions quietly drift apart.

items.prompt: A bug is found in how order totals are calculated. In a codebase where /v1 and /v2 are both thin adapters over one shared core function, how many places need the fix?
choices: One — the shared core
Two — once per version
Zero — versions are independent by design
It depends on which version is newer
items.explanation: Because both adapters delegate the actual calculation to the same core function, fixing it there fixes it for every version's adapter simultaneously. This is the entire benefit of the pattern over maintaining separate codebases per version.
items.reference:
🧩 /v1 and /v2 adapters both call the SAME shared core logic
🛠️ A bug fix in core applies to both versions at once

Why: forking the codebase per version means every future fix has to be applied N times, and versions quietly drift apart.

items.prompt: What's the main long-term risk of maintaining a fully separate codebase per API version instead of thin adapters over a shared core?
choices: Versions quietly drift apart as fixes and rules get applied inconsistently across copies
The server becomes faster
Old versions become impossible to deprecate
There's no risk — separate codebases are simpler
items.explanation: Every fix, security patch, or business-rule change now has to be remembered and reapplied in N places. In practice this drifts — some versions get a fix, others are forgotten — until versions behave inconsistently in ways nobody intended.
items.reference:
🧩 /v1 and /v2 adapters both call the SAME shared core logic
🛠️ A bug fix in core applies to both versions at once

Why: forking the codebase per version means every future fix has to be applied N times, and versions quietly drift apart.

items.prompt: Does marking a GraphQL field @deprecated stop it from resolving when an old client queries it?
choices: No — the resolver still runs and returns real data until the field is actually removed
Yes — it immediately returns null
Yes — the query fails with an error
It depends on the GraphQL server version
items.explanation: @deprecated is metadata for tooling (IDE warnings, introspection, codegen) — it doesn't change runtime behavior at all. The field's resolver keeps executing normally until someone deletes the field/resolver itself.
items.reference:
@deprecated

Tooling/docs hint only — field still resolves

Deleting the resolver

Actually removes the field — breaks old clients now

Why: deprecation announces intent to remove later; only deleting the field/resolver actually removes it.

items.prompt: What is @deprecated primarily useful for?
choices: Surfacing a retirement warning in developer tooling (IDEs, codegen, schema docs) without breaking anyone yet
Automatically migrating old clients to the new field
Blocking new clients from using the old field
Reducing the field's response size
items.explanation: It's a signal aimed at developers building against the schema — it shows up as a warning in tooling — while leaving the field fully functional for whoever is still using it. It communicates intent to remove later, nothing more.
items.reference:
@deprecated

Tooling/docs hint only — field still resolves

Deleting the resolver

Actually removes the field — breaks old clients now

Why: deprecation announces intent to remove later; only deleting the field/resolver actually removes it.

items.prompt: When is it actually safe to delete a deprecated field's resolver?
choices: After monitoring shows real usage of that field has dropped to zero (or the announced sunset date has passed with usage confirmed gone)
As soon as the @deprecated directive is added
After the next deploy, regardless of usage
Never — deprecated fields must stay forever
items.explanation: Deprecation announces intent; deletion executes it. Skipping the monitoring step between them is exactly how a field that 'should' be unused turns out to still have real traffic — and breaks it the moment it's deleted.
items.reference:
@deprecated

Tooling/docs hint only — field still resolves

Deleting the resolver

Actually removes the field — breaks old clients now

Why: deprecation announces intent to remove later; only deleting the field/resolver actually removes it.

items.prompt: Which of these is a common place a REST API's version lives?
choices: The URL path, e.g. /v2/users
Inside the response body's first field
The HTTP method used
The client's User-Agent string
items.explanation: URL-path versioning (/v1/, /v2/) and a versioned Accept/media-type header are the two most common places REST carries a version — both are part of the request itself, visible before the server even processes the body.
items.reference:
🔗 URL path: /v1/users, /v2/users
📨 Header: Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json
🚫 GraphQL: neither — one schema, evolved additively

Why: REST needs somewhere to carry the version since the URL/headers ARE the contract's public surface; GraphQL's surface is the schema itself.

items.prompt: Does a typical GraphQL API put a version number in its endpoint URL the way REST does?
choices: No — GraphQL usually has a single endpoint and evolves one schema additively instead
Yes — /graphql/v1, /graphql/v2 is the standard pattern
Only for mutations, not queries
Yes, but only for breaking changes to scalars
items.explanation: GraphQL's usual design keeps one endpoint and one schema; instead of standing up a parallel URL per version, it adds new fields/types and deprecates retiring ones. There's no second deployment to route between — deprecation is schema metadata, not a fork.
items.reference:
🔗 URL path: /v1/users, /v2/users
📨 Header: Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json
🚫 GraphQL: neither — one schema, evolved additively

Why: REST needs somewhere to carry the version since the URL/headers ARE the contract's public surface; GraphQL's surface is the schema itself.

items.prompt: A mobile screen needs a user's name and their last order's total — nothing else. Against a REST GET /users/:id that always returns the full user object, what's happening?
choices: Over-fetching — the client receives far more fields than the screen displays
Under-fetching — not enough data is returned
A breaking change occurred
The endpoint is misconfigured
items.explanation: The endpoint's response shape is fixed regardless of what the caller actually needs, so the client always gets the full object — including every field the screen has no use for. GraphQL avoids this by letting the query select just name and the order total.
items.reference:
📦 REST: fixed shape per endpoint — get everything or make another request
🎯 GraphQL: client selects exact fields, any nesting depth, one request

Why: a fixed-shape endpoint either over-fetches (more than the screen needs) or under-fetches (forces more round trips) — GraphQL's per-query field selection avoids both.

items.prompt: A screen needs a user, their orders, and each order's line items. Built against a REST API with one endpoint per resource, why does this typically require multiple sequential requests (a waterfall)?
choices: Each REST endpoint returns a fixed shape for one resource type — nested data isn't included unless a specific endpoint is built for that exact combination
REST doesn't support nested data at all, ever
The server intentionally throttles requests
REST always requires authentication per request
items.explanation: Without a purpose-built endpoint for this exact combination, the client has to fetch the user, then loop over orders to fetch each one's line items — an N+1 pattern. GraphQL's single query with nested field selection avoids building a new endpoint for every combination screens need.
items.reference:
📦 REST: fixed shape per endpoint — get everything or make another request
🎯 GraphQL: client selects exact fields, any nesting depth, one request

Why: a fixed-shape endpoint either over-fetches (more than the screen needs) or under-fetches (forces more round trips) — GraphQL's per-query field selection avoids both.

items.prompt: What's the core trade-off a fixed-shape REST endpoint makes, compared to GraphQL's per-query field selection?
choices: Either return more than a given screen needs (over-fetch) or force multiple requests to get enough (under-fetch)
REST endpoints are always slower over the network
REST can't return JSON, only XML
GraphQL responses are always smaller regardless of what's queried
items.explanation: A fixed shape has to pick one size that serves every caller — screens that need less get over-fetching, screens that need more (nested data not in that shape) get under-fetching and extra round trips. Field selection per query sidesteps the trade-off by tailoring the response to each caller.
items.reference:
📦 REST: fixed shape per endpoint — get everything or make another request
🎯 GraphQL: client selects exact fields, any nesting depth, one request

Why: a fixed-shape endpoint either over-fetches (more than the screen needs) or under-fetches (forces more round trips) — GraphQL's per-query field selection avoids both.

items.prompt: In the deprecation flow (ship new -> announce -> monitor usage -> remove), what's the purpose of the monitor-usage step specifically?
choices: To verify real traffic has actually stopped depending on the old field/version before removing it, since not every client will act on an announcement
To measure server response time
To decide which team owns the migration
To generate documentation automatically
items.explanation: An announced sunset date is a plan, not proof every caller has moved off the old contract — some are unattended scripts or abandoned integrations that will never see the announcement. Monitoring turns 'we announced it' into 'we verified it's actually safe' before removal.
items.reference:
1. Ship new field/version
2. Announce + sunset date
3. Monitor real usage
4. Remove once usage ≈ 0

Why: an announced date is a plan, not proof every caller acted on it — monitoring turns the plan into a verified safe removal.

items.prompt: What's the correct order of the deprecation steps: ship the replacement, announce a sunset date, monitor real usage, remove the old field/version?
choices: Ship replacement -> announce sunset date -> monitor usage -> remove
Announce sunset date -> remove -> ship replacement -> monitor usage
Remove -> ship replacement -> announce -> monitor
Monitor usage -> ship replacement -> remove -> announce
items.explanation: The replacement has to exist before anyone can migrate to it; the announcement sets expectations and a target date; monitoring confirms the migration actually happened before the final, irreversible removal step.
items.reference:
1. Ship new field/version
2. Announce + sunset date
3. Monitor real usage
4. Remove once usage ≈ 0

Why: an announced date is a plan, not proof every caller acted on it — monitoring turns the plan into a verified safe removal.

items.prompt: Implement findRemovedFields(oldSchema, newSchema): return an array of field names present in oldSchema but missing from newSchema. Example: oldSchema = { temperature: 'number', cityId: 'string' }, newSchema = { tempF: 'number', cityId: 'string' } should detect that 'temperature' was removed.

tests.description: detects a removed field
returns empty array when nothing removed
tests.expr: expect(findRemovedFields({ a: 'string', b: 'number' }, { a: 'string', b: 'number', c: 'boolean' })).toEqual([])

tests.description: detects multiple removed fields

items.explanation: Walk every key that existed in the old schema and keep the ones missing from the new schema — that's exactly the definition of 'removed.' Fields only present in the new schema (additions) are irrelevant here since the loop never visits them, matching L1's rule that additions alone are never breaking.
items.reference:
Question: which fields disappeared between two schema snapshots?

Why: a removed field is the sharpest kind of breaking change — any client reading it gets undefined immediately.

items.prompt: Implement findRemovedFields(oldSchema, newSchema) the same way, applied to a user-profile endpoint. Example: oldSchema = { username: 'string', email: 'string' }, newSchema = { handle: 'string', email: 'string' } should detect that 'username' was removed.

tests.description: detects a renamed-away field
returns empty array when nothing removed
detects multiple removed fields

items.explanation: Walk every key that existed in the old schema and keep the ones missing from the new schema. A rename is functionally a removal-plus-addition from an old client's point of view, so 'username' shows up as removed even though 'handle' now covers the same idea.
items.reference:
Question: which fields disappeared between two schema snapshots?

Why: a removed field is the sharpest kind of breaking change — any client reading it gets undefined immediately.

items.prompt: Implement findRemovedFields(oldSchema, newSchema) applied to a product endpoint. Example: oldSchema = { price: 'number', sku: 'string' }, newSchema = { priceCents: 'number', sku: 'string' } should detect that 'price' was removed.

tests.description: detects a removed field
returns empty array when nothing removed
detects multiple removed fields

items.explanation: Walk every key that existed in the old schema and keep the ones missing from the new schema — that's exactly the definition of 'removed,' regardless of whether the replacement field's name is related or not.
items.reference:
Question: which fields disappeared between two schema snapshots?

Why: a removed field is the sharpest kind of breaking change — any client reading it gets undefined immediately.

items.prompt: Implement findTypeChanges(oldSchema, newSchema): for every field present in BOTH schemas, if its type differs, include { field, from, to } in the result array. Fields only present in one schema should be ignored (that's a removal/addition, not a type change). Example: oldSchema = { id: 'string', age: 'number' }, newSchema = { id: 'string', age: 'string' } should return [{ field: 'age', from: 'number', to: 'string' }].

tests.description: detects a type change on a shared field
tests.expr: expect(findTypeChanges({ id: 'string', age: 'number' }, { id: 'string', age: 'string' })).toEqual([{ field: 'age', from: 'number', to: 'string' }])

tests.description: returns empty array when types match
ignores fields not present in both schemas

items.explanation: Only fields present in both schemas can have a 'type change' — a field missing from one side is a removal or addition, a separate category of change. For the fields that survive in both, compare old and new type strings directly and record the ones that differ.
items.reference:
Question: did a field's type change between two schema snapshots (only checked where the field exists in both)?

Why: old client parsing/validation logic assumes the old type — a silent type change breaks it just as hard as a removal.

items.prompt: Implement findTypeChanges(oldSchema, newSchema) applied to an order endpoint. Example: oldSchema = { quantity: 'number', note: 'string' }, newSchema = { quantity: 'string', note: 'string' } should return [{ field: 'quantity', from: 'number', to: 'string' }].

tests.description: detects a type change on a shared field
tests.expr: expect(findTypeChanges({ quantity: 'number', note: 'string' }, { quantity: 'string', note: 'string' })).toEqual([{ field: 'quantity', from: 'number', to: 'string' }])

tests.description: returns empty array when types match
ignores fields not present in both schemas

items.explanation: Only fields present in both schemas can have a 'type change.' For the fields that survive in both, compare old and new type strings directly and record the ones that differ — a field that disappeared entirely (like 'tax' or 'discount' here) is a different category of change, handled by findRemovedFields instead.
items.reference:
Question: did a field's type change between two schema snapshots (only checked where the field exists in both)?

Why: old client parsing/validation logic assumes the old type — a silent type change breaks it just as hard as a removal.

items.prompt: Implement becameRequired(oldSchema, newSchema): both schemas map field names to { required: boolean }. Return the names of fields that were optional (required: false) in oldSchema and became required (required: true) in newSchema. Fields that went the other way (required to optional) should NOT be included — only tightening the constraint counts. Example: oldSchema = { cityId: { required: true }, notes: { required: false } }, newSchema = { cityId: { required: true }, notes: { required: true } } should return ['notes'].

tests.description: detects a field that became required
tests.expr: expect(becameRequired({ cityId: { required: true }, notes: { required: false } }, { cityId: { required: true }, notes: { required: true } })).toEqual(['notes'])

tests.description: does not flag the loosening direction
tests.expr: expect(becameRequired({ a: { required: true } }, { a: { required: false } })).toEqual([])

tests.description: detects multiple fields that became required
tests.expr: expect(becameRequired({ a: { required: false }, b: { required: false } }, { a: { required: true }, b: { required: true } })).toEqual(['a', 'b'])

items.explanation: Only the optional-to-required direction rejects requests that used to succeed — a required-to-optional change loosens a constraint and can't break an old client, since old clients already always sent that field. The check has to be directional, not just 'required changed.'
items.reference:
Question: did a field go from optional to required (the unsafe direction only)?

Why: required-to-optional loosens a promise (safe); optional-to-required tightens it and rejects requests old clients used to be able to make.

items.prompt: Implement becameRequired(oldSchema, newSchema) applied to a signup form's fields. Example: oldSchema = { email: { required: true }, phone: { required: false } }, newSchema = { email: { required: true }, phone: { required: true } } should return ['phone'].

tests.description: detects a field that became required
tests.expr: expect(becameRequired({ email: { required: true }, phone: { required: false } }, { email: { required: true }, phone: { required: true } })).toEqual(['phone'])

tests.description: does not flag the loosening direction
tests.expr: expect(becameRequired({ referralCode: { required: true } }, { referralCode: { required: false } })).toEqual([])

tests.description: returns empty array when nothing tightened
tests.expr: expect(becameRequired({ email: { required: true } }, { email: { required: true } })).toEqual([])

items.explanation: Only the optional-to-required direction matters — it rejects signups that used to succeed without a phone number. Loosening a field (referralCode here) or leaving it unchanged never breaks an old client, so neither should be flagged.
items.reference:
Question: did a field go from optional to required (the unsafe direction only)?

Why: required-to-optional loosens a promise (safe); optional-to-required tightens it and rejects requests old clients used to be able to make.

items.prompt: Implement becameRequired(oldSchema, newSchema) applied to an order-creation endpoint. Example: oldSchema = { items: { required: true }, giftMessage: { required: false } }, newSchema = { items: { required: true }, giftMessage: { required: false } } should return [] (nothing tightened).

tests.description: returns empty array when nothing tightened
tests.expr: expect(becameRequired({ items: { required: true }, giftMessage: { required: false } }, { items: { required: true }, giftMessage: { required: false } })).toEqual([])

tests.description: detects a field that became required
tests.expr: expect(becameRequired({ giftMessage: { required: false } }, { giftMessage: { required: true } })).toEqual(['giftMessage'])

tests.description: does not flag the loosening direction
tests.expr: expect(becameRequired({ items: { required: true } }, { items: { required: false } })).toEqual([])

items.explanation: The check is directional: only flag a field moving from required: false to required: true. Anything that stays the same or loosens should never appear in the result, since neither of those can reject a request an old client used to be able to send.
items.reference:
Question: did a field go from optional to required (the unsafe direction only)?

Why: required-to-optional loosens a promise (safe); optional-to-required tightens it and rejects requests old clients used to be able to make.

items.prompt: A shared core function getReading(cityId) is already given, returning { celsius }. celsiusToFahrenheit is also given. Implement handleV2Weather(cityId) that returns { tempF, tempC } by calling getReading and celsiusToFahrenheit — without re-implementing the lookup or the conversion math inline.

tests.description: converts city-1's reading correctly
converts city-2's reading correctly

items.explanation: The point isn't just getting the right numbers — it's getting them by calling the shared getReading and celsiusToFahrenheit functions rather than duplicating the lookup or the conversion formula inline. That's what keeps a future fix to either one automatically correct here too, matching L2/L3's shared-core-plus-adapters pattern.
items.reference:
Question: can a new version's response shape be built by calling the SAME core logic as the old version, with no duplicated conversion logic?

Why: thin adapters over one shared core mean a fix applies everywhere at once — the pattern from L2/L3's main example.

items.prompt: The same getReading(cityId) and celsiusToFahrenheit are given. Implement handleV1Weather(cityId) that returns the OLD shape, { temperature }, still expressed in Fahrenheit — by calling getReading and celsiusToFahrenheit, not by re-implementing them.

items.prompt: Implement decideVersionBump(breakingChangeCount, newFieldCount): if there's at least one breaking change, return 'MAJOR'. Otherwise, if at least one new field was added, return 'MINOR'. Otherwise return 'PATCH'.

additive-only change is MINOR
no observable change is PATCH
breaking changes win even alongside additive ones

items.explanation: The precedence matters: any breaking change forces MAJOR regardless of how many additive changes also shipped in the same release — a single removed field can't be offset by five new ones. Only when there are zero breaking changes does the additive count decide MINOR vs. PATCH.

Why: tying a contract-diff check's output directly to MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH is what turns 'we checked' into a number clients can actually plan around.
